title: Australia's Resource Wealth Giveaway: How weak public capture leaves billions in revenue on the table (Wielga, Prosper Australia Research Institute, October 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full PDF (8.6 MB, one request, HTTP success) saved to fetched/wielga.pdf; pdftotext extraction (layout and raw) read for the executive summary (pp. 3-5), chs. 1-7 (pp. 6-37), Appendices A, B, D (pp. 38-59) and the Table 6 / Appendix E double-loss section; reference list (pp. 67-72) scanned for primary URLs. Landing page not separately requested. Appendices C and E tables and most of the reference list were skimmed, not read line by line.
verdict_reason: Substantive, openly accessible, methodologically transparent (formula, numerators, denominators, windows and sensitivities all disclosed in Appendices B and D). It is a new commissioned Prosper report (2026, petroleum/mining; different author and scope from the 2013 TRRA), and the wiki has no coverage of Wielga, the public-capture ratio, Queensland's post-2022 coal royalty outcome, or the A$45bn claim. Precedent (research/total-resource-rents-australia.md) is a standalone research page with status stated; carry the same way: Tier 2 commissioned estimate, figures attributed to the report, Tier 1 primaries cited for any fact stated in the wiki's own voice. Then cross-link from organizations/prosper-australia.md (Work list), research/australia-mining-royalties-prrt.md and research/nassios-australia-lng-prrt-structural-limits.md (See Also / Bears On), and places/australia.md (which currently has no resource-royalty content). Not an ENRICH: too large and self-contained for a section on any existing page.
claim_grade: B-claim (Tier 2 for the report's own calculations and policy conclusions; the report is advocacy-commissioned, not peer-reviewed). Quoted official inputs (ATO, ABS, Queensland Budget papers, Alaska Dept of Revenue, Norwegian Ministry/Offshore Directorate, Petoro) are A-claim only when read from the primary itself, which this brief did not do.
content_summary: AUTHOR/COMMISSION (p.1): 'Richard Wielga is an independent economist and policy consultant, commissioned by the Prosper Australia Research Institute to deliver this report.' Six years as economist at Victoria's Dept of Treasury and Finance, later senior Victorian Public Service roles; BA Economics/Political Science, University of Melbourne. Prosper described as 'founded in the Georgist tradition'. Report is dated October 2026; data cut-off 14 September 2026 (App. B, p.39). Authorship is commissioned-by-advocacy: Tier 2 per people-tiers.json for Prosper; Wielga is a Tier 2 practitioner-consultant (not in tiers file).

DEFINITION (Box 3, p.15; App. B.1, p.39): public-capture ratio = public resource revenue collected / resource-sector gross value added. 'Public revenue includes taxes, royalties and similar public charges'; numerator counts national plus state/provincial layers (company income tax attributable to the sector, royalties, fees). Ratio of 10-year totals (not mean of annual ratios), real prices; 'A 10-year period is used where possible'. Adapted from Davies & Schroder (2025), Aust. J. Agric. Resource Econ. 69(1), 'government take' (fn 11, p.15). Report's own caveats (p.43): it is 'a value share, not a rent or profit share'; mixed accounting bases; does not control for cost structures; all figures 'indicative'.

AUSTRALIA DATA SOURCES (App. B.2, pp.40-43, Tables B1-B5): denominator = ABS National Accounts current-price GVA for the ABS 'Mining' industry (oil/gas, coal, metal ore, non-metallic, exploration/support), split into mining-only and petroleum-only using shares from ABS Australian Industry IVA, so the splits are 'constructed proxies rather than separately published ABS series' (p.16). Numerator = ATO Taxation Statistics 2023-24 company tax payable by fine industry; state mineral royalties from EY (2025) report for the Minerals Council (Table 1); PRRT cash receipts from Final Budget Outcomes; petroleum production excise/royalties/fees from APPEA/Australian Energy Producers surveys (industry body). Window 2014-15 to 2023-24 (2024-25 excluded, ATO data unavailable), CPI-deflated to 2023-24 prices.

HEADLINE AUSTRALIAN RATIOS (Table B4, p.43): full resources 22.7% (23%) = A$531.3bn / A$2,340.4bn; mining-only 25.7% (26%) = A$448.0bn / A$1,745.6bn; petroleum-only 14.0% (14%) = A$83.3bn / A$594.8bn. Table B5: petroleum numerator = company tax A$37.9bn + PRRT A$14.7bn + production excise/royalties/fees A$30.8bn (10-year, 2023-24 prices); mining numerator = company tax A$258.8bn + royalties A$189.2bn. NB the 14% is total government take on the sector (company tax included), not PRRT-only.

PEERS (Table 2 p.19; App. B.3-B.7): Alaska 42.2% (US$31.6bn / US$74.8bn, 2015-24; includes an ESTIMATED federal corporate income tax scaled from state CIT by the 21%/9.4% statutory ratio, 'order-of-magnitude'; without it 38.8%, Table B11 p.49). Norway headline 39.6% (40%) 'private-operator' benchmark, 2016-25: numerator NOK 2,992.6bn = ordinary and special petroleum taxes, royalties, environmental taxes, area fees; EXCLUDES SDFI net cash flow and Equinor dividends; denominator NOK 7,558.7bn = petroleum GVA with the state's SDFI share removed using Petoro's reserve-share proxy (about 30-33%). Full-capture Norway 50.5%; tax-and-fee-only with unadjusted denominator 27.4% (Table B8 p.46, Box 4 pp.17-18). The 40% therefore rests on a denominator adjustment the report calls 'not a perfect' proxy (reserve share, not GVA share); sensitivity dropping environmental taxes/area fees gives 38.3% (p.47). Mining peers: Chile 11.5% (2 yrs 2024-25), Peru 11.2% (includes an estimated employee profit-share levy that is not public revenue; 9.4% without), Quebec about 8% (2014-21).

ANSWER TO 'ADJUSTED': Norway about 40% is adjusted by removing state-ownership returns from the numerator AND the SDFI footprint from the denominator (Box 4, p.18: 'Option 3 (preferred): Norway private-operator benchmark - 40%'). Alaska 42% is not adjusted for cost structure.

QUEENSLAND TIERS (p.8-9, citing Queensland Revenue Office 2026b): from 1 July 2022 marginal rates 7% on first $100/t, 12.5% $100-150, 15% $150-175, 20% $175-225, 30% $225-300, 40% above $300/t. 'Prior to 1 July 2022, the highest Queensland coal rate was 15% on the portion above $150/t.' (Scanner's '7% rising to 40% above $300/t' is right but they are marginal bands, as the report states.)

QUEENSLAND 41% (App. B.5, pp.49-51, Table B14): headline 40.6% (41%) = A$44.7bn / A$110.1bn over only THREE years (2022-23 to 2024-25), 'in a strong coal-price period'. Numerator = observed Queensland coal royalties (Qld Budget Strategy and Outlook, BP2, actuals) plus an ESTIMATED coal company tax (ATO national coal CIT apportioned by Queensland's export-value share; 2024-25 CIT itself estimated by scaling 2023-24 by operating profit before tax). Denominator is a proxy: ABS Australian coal IVA x Queensland export-value share (IVA, not National Accounts GVA, so basis differs from the Australian ratios). Two-year cross-check 41.7%; ten-year context 2015-16 to 2024-25 = 30.0%. The report itself says (pp.21-22, 27) the 3-year window is short and the benchmark 'does not map perfectly' to broader mining.

QUEENSLAND INVESTMENT STATEMENT (ch.4, pp.23-26, Fig. 5): Qld saleable coal 'around 222-224 Mt' post-reform; active mines 53 (2021-22) to 60 (2024-25) vs NSW 40 to 37; Qld coal employment about 26,000 (four-quarter average to Feb 2026, ABS), 'broadly in line with pre-reform level'; NSW up from about 15,000 to 17,500. No investment series exists at state-coal level ('Comparable state-level coal investment data are not publicly available', p.24), so investment is NOT measured directly; conclusion is 'industry's strongest reform warnings were not borne out'. The report concedes the 2025 BHP Mitsubishi Alliance Saraji South 750 job cuts and Qld Resources Council claims, and says closures may reflect prices/costs (p.25); NSW also raised coal royalties 2.6 points from 1 July 2024, so it is an imperfect comparator. Footnote 22 notes Qld published 2025-26 data on 17 Sept 2026 showing stable production despite a lower mine count.

A$45BN DERIVATION (ch.5 Table 4 p.27; App. D Tables D1-D2 pp.58-59): counterfactual = (benchmark ratio minus Australian baseline ratio) x Australian 10-year sector GVA, divided by 10, converted to June 2026 prices (factor 1.0732). Mining: (40.60% - 25.66%) x A$1,745.6bn = A$260.7bn/10 = A$26.1bn (2023-24 prices) = A$28.0bn (June 2026). Petroleum: (39.59% - 14.01%) x A$594.8bn = A$152.2bn/10 -> A$16.3bn (Norway); (42.25% - 14.01%) -> A$168.0bn/10 -> A$18.0bn (Alaska). Combined A$44.3bn (Norway) to A$46.0bn (Alaska); 'around $45 billion'. Norway and Alaska are alternatives, not added. Static: holds GVA constant, no behavioural, investment or cost response (p.59). The mining line applies a 3-year Queensland COAL ratio (which includes estimated company tax) to ALL Australian mining (iron ore, gold, critical minerals); the report flags this (pp.27-28). A$45bn is thus a gap in total government take on a GVA base, not a forecast of new royalty receipts, and is across Commonwealth and state revenue streams. Domestic comparison: petroleum at Australia's own mining ratio would be about A$7bn/yr higher (p.28; not in the A$45bn).

PRRT DESIGN (pp.9-11, 14, 21; Box 6): the report says the PRRT is a 40% tax on super-profits that 'looks strong on paper' but 'has not produced strong and timely revenues, and current forecasts show no sustained improvement' (p.11, citing Treasury 2023 pp.7-8 and Budget 2026-27 BP1 pp.201, 208). The only design mechanism named is that LNG's 'very large upfront capital investment and long payback periods ... can delay tax payments and reduce observed public capture, especially when deductions are carried forward over long periods' (p.21, citing Treasury 2023 pp.12-13, 38-39). The report does NOT discuss uplift rates, the Residual Pricing Method, the 2024 deductions cap, or the A$282.6bn carry-forward stock; it also explicitly says it 'does not design a new Commonwealth petroleum tax' (p.5). It says the low petroleum ratio may partly reflect LNG's higher cost structure but that Norway and Alaska are not low-cost either (Box 6, p.21).

POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS (Exec summary p.5; ch.7 pp.35-37): 1a market-linked state royalties - base rate per commodity adjusting with price relative to a rolling 10-year median (Box 9 p.35: if iron ore had a 7.5% base rate and price were twice its 10-year median, rate would rise to 15%; from Prosper's 2024 'Rent-Controlled Resources'); 1b hybrid floor plus boom-sensitive component (Alaska/Queensland as examples); 2 address petroleum under-capture at Commonwealth level, judged against the principle that public returns should rise with prices and profits. Explicitly 'does not recommend that Australia establish a state-owned resource company' (p.31). Slogan: 'Low, flat royalties are policy choices.'

DOUBLE LOSS (ch.6 pp.29-34, Tables 5-7): ownership-weighted direct foreign state-linked production value about A$15.9bn (mining A$7.0bn, LNG A$8.9bn) = 3.9% of 2024-25 resource and energy exports; applying 3.9% proportionally to the A$44-46bn gap gives A$1.7-1.8bn (rounded 'almost $2 billion') a year (Table 7, p.34). Report states it is 'illustrative', does not match mining/petroleum exposure shares to their gaps, excludes portfolio holdings (Chinalco/Rio) and does not estimate actual profits transferred. Treat as the weakest figure in the report (proportional allocation of a counterfactual to ownership shares of production value).

MINING 26% 'above peers, flat, not boom-sensitive' (Fig. 4 p.19, p.21): report says mining 25.7% is higher than Chile/Peru/Quebec and 'surprising', offers untested explanations (iron ore/coal volume, peer regimes narrower than design suggests, administration), and says it is 'not obviously weak'. Design rated 'Low' boom sensitivity because state royalties about 5-10% are flat (Table 1 p.14). The A$45bn is therefore driven more by the Queensland-coal benchmark than by a weak-observed-capture finding for mining.

existing_wiki_coverage: No page on Wielga, the 2026 report, the public-capture ratio, or Prosper's 2024 Rent-Controlled Resources (grep zero). organizations/prosper-australia.md (40 lines) lists TRRA 2013 and speculative vacancies only. research/total-resource-rents-australia.md is the 2013 Fitzgerald report (23.6% of GDP; 40% EBITDAX; it notes an effective PRRT rate of 3.2%); it is the structural precedent for carrying a Prosper report. research/australia-mining-royalties-prrt.md mentions Queensland's 2022 tiered coal royalty only qualitatively ('rates escalate sharply once prices cross defined thresholds'), carries ATO PRRT payable $1,996.6m (2021-22), $1,867.1m (2022-23), $1,483.3m (2023-24), $1.87bn (2024-25), Budget cash receipts $1,420m (2024-25), and the A$282.6bn carry-forward (ATO evidence via Greens' comments). research/nassios-australia-lng-prrt-structural-limits.md carries PRRT revenue A$1.5bn (2014) to A$2.3bn (2023) vs a rent proxy A$4.6bn to A$18.1bn = about 15%, Norway about 48%, and the uplift/carry-forward and transfer-pricing mechanisms. places/australia.md has no PRRT, royalty or coal content (grep: only Queensland land-tax and a planner). TENSIONS TO HANDLE: (1) Nassios about 15% is PRRT collections divided by a resource-depletion rent proxy (a rent-capture rate); Wielga 14% is all government take on the petroleum sector (company tax, PRRT, excise/royalties) divided by sector GVA (a value-share). The near-equal numbers are coincidental and not comparable; likewise Nassios's Norway about 48% (PRRT-comparable regime) vs Wielga's 40% (taxes/GVA, SDFI-adjusted). Do not present them as corroborating each other. (2) Wielga's PRRT series is A$14.7bn over ten years in 2023-24 prices (about A$1.5bn/yr real) from Final Budget Outcome cash receipts; it is of the same order as the wiki's ATO payable and Budget cash series but is on a different basis and is not a drop-in replacement. (3) Wielga does not mention the A$282.6bn carry-forward or the 2024 deductions cap; its PRRT discussion is thinner than the wiki's two existing pages, and it dates the PRRT as a 'forecasts show no sustained improvement' note citing Budget 2026-27, which agrees with the wiki's Budget-estimate series (A$1.4bn 2025-26, A$1.9bn 2026-27, falling to A$1.25bn by 2029-30). (4) The wiki's Queensland-onshore-gas point (Kraal: PRRT-equivalent arrangements raised nothing; conventional royalty reintroduced) is consistent with Wielga's note that Queensland has had a volume-based price-linked petroleum royalty since 1 October 2020 (p.9, citing QRO 2026a) - useful corroboration for the same fact, from a different source.
scanner_premise_errors: Scanner says 'the PRRT's design (uplift rates, carried-forward deductions) has not produced strong observed revenue'. The report does not discuss uplift at all (no occurrence of 'uplift' in the text); it only mentions carried-forward deductions once, in Box 6 (p.21), as a cost-structure/LNG-payback reason. The uplift/carry-forward mechanism is on the wiki via Nassios, not via Wielga.

Scanner says 'Queensland coal post-2022-reform about 41% ... no investment collapse' and calls it 'the domestic proof point'. The 41% is a three-year window in a strong coal-price period, built with an ESTIMATED company-tax numerator and a proxy IVA denominator; the report's own ten-year Queensland ratio is 30.0%. The report also says investment 'cannot be measured directly' (no state coal capex series) - the 'no investment collapse' finding is from production, active-mine counts and employment, not investment. 'Proof point' is the scanner's phrasing; the report says 'not a perfect benchmark' and that the 'evidence window ... is short'.

Scanner says 'mining about 26% but flat, not boom-sensitive': the 26% is a company-tax-plus-royalty take on GVA (not royalties alone) and the report treats it as 'not obviously weak' and above Chile/Peru/Quebec; the 'flat' is a statement about design (royalties of about 5-10%), not about the observed 26% ratio. The ratio is not shown to be flat over time.

Scanner says 'about 10-year windows': true only for Australia (2014-15 to 2023-24), Norway (2016-25), Alaska and Peru (2015-24); Queensland is 3 years, Chile 2, Quebec 8 (Table 2, p.19). The Australian and Norwegian windows are not aligned.
Scanner says 'primary resolved via web search' / landing-page verified live; the PDF was reachable with a single ordinary request here and extracted cleanly. No access problem.

Scanner says '$16bn direct foreign state-linked production value means under-capture leaks to foreign public' - the report's double-loss figure is a 3.9% proportional allocation of the A$44-46bn gap = A$1.7-1.8bn/yr ('almost $2 billion'), explicitly 'illustrative' and not an estimate of profits transferred (Box 7, Table 7). Also, Norway '40% adjusted' is the report's own SDFI-removed private-operator ratio, not an official Norwegian figure; the scanner's phrase is otherwise accurate.
uncertainties: Page locators are printed page numbers; the PDF's page index may be offset by about one page for pdftotext output. Quotes were checked against the extracted text only.

Figures were not recomputed from the primary data; only the report's internal arithmetic was spot-checked (Table D2: (40.60-25.66)% x 1,745.6 = 260.7; (39.59-14.01)% x 594.8 = 152.2; (42.25-14.01)% x 594.8 = 168.0; all reproduce). The A$44.3bn/A$46.0bn totals sum correctly.

Whether the wiki should carry any of the capture ratios as fact: the Australian ratio rests on a constructed denominator split (IVA shares applied to National Accounts GVA) and a petroleum numerator component from an industry body (Australian Energy Producers). Alaska includes an estimated federal CIT; Norway depends on a reserve-share proxy; Queensland depends on estimated CIT and proxy IVA. Only the Alaska state revenue, Norway cash-flow, ATO and Queensland royalty inputs are official series; the ratios are Prosper's/Wielga's constructs.

Cross-check of Queensland royalty receipts, ATO coal/oil-gas company tax and PRRT cash receipts against the primaries was not done here; T1 should do it before the wiki states any Queensland revenue figure in its own voice.

The report is not peer-reviewed; no independent reception (industry response, Treasury, academic) was sought. Claim that proactiveinvestors.com.au carried a news wrapper on 22 Oct 2026 was not checked (not needed).
Wielga is not in people-tiers.json; treat as Tier 2 (commissioned consultant, advocacy report), a prior ex-Treasury-and-Finance role notwithstanding.
Prosper's own 2024 'Rent-Controlled Resources' report (variable royalty model) is the source of the recommendation and is not on the wiki; consider a separate T0 item.
suggested_text: Prosper Australia's 2026 report *Australia's Resource Wealth Giveaway*, written by the independent economist Richard Wielga on commission from the Prosper Australia Research Institute, compares Australia's resource take with Norway, Alaska, Chile, Peru, Quebec and Queensland coal using a 'public-capture ratio': public revenue collected from a sector (company tax, royalties, resource taxes and related charges, at national and state level) divided by that sector's gross value added, summed over about ten years where data allow. On the report's calculation, Australia's petroleum ratio is about 14% (2014-15 to 2023-24), against about 42% for Alaska and about 40% for a Norwegian benchmark that excludes state-ownership returns and the state's direct-interest share of activity; Australia's mining ratio is about 26%, above the report's mining peers; and Queensland coal, under the tiered royalty introduced on 1 July 2022 (marginal rates from 7% to 40% above A$300 a tonne), reaches about 41% over its first three post-reform years. Applying the Queensland-coal benchmark to Australian mining and the Norwegian or Alaskan benchmark to petroleum, the report estimates about A$45 billion a year of additional public revenue (A$44-46 billion). The report describes these figures as indicative: the mining and petroleum denominators are constructed proxies rather than published series, the Queensland and Alaskan numerators include estimated company tax, the ratios do not control for cost structures, and the revenue estimate holds production and investment constant. It argues that Queensland's coal sector has not contracted relative to New South Wales on production, active mines and employment (state-level coal investment data are not available), and recommends market-linked or hybrid state royalties and Commonwealth petroleum-tax reform. The report is an advocacy-commissioned estimate and has not been peer reviewed. [Source line, Sources only: Wielga (2026), Prosper Australia Research Institute, PDF, full text read at last review (2026-11-20); B-claim, Tier 2; official inputs (ABS, ATO, Queensland budget papers, Alaska Department of Revenue, Norwegian Offshore Directorate) not independently re-checked.] For facts stated in the wiki's own voice (the Queensland royalty bands, PRRT receipts, Queensland coal royalty revenue), cite the Queensland Revenue Office schedule, the ATO/Budget series and the Queensland Budget Papers directly.
